subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Salivary glands produce secretions that protect the oral cavity and act as a mucosal immune site (MALT). In low‑resource settings, clinicians must recognise infectious, autoimmune and obstructive diseases, use limited investigations, and manage complications promptly.
aka: Mucosal associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) of the mouth

sections.p: Three paired major glands (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) plus numerous minor glands line the oral mucosa. They secrete water, electrolytes, mucins, amylase, lysozyme and secretory IgA, forming the first line of defence against oral pathogens.
The glandular epithelium houses organized lymphoid aggregates (MALT). Secretory IgA is produced locally and neutralises bacteria and viruses before they colonise teeth or the pharynx.
b: IgA deficiency predisposes to recurrent oral candidiasis and dental caries
Lysozyme and lactoferrin provide bactericidal activity

sections.p: Pathogens reach the glands by retrograde ductal spread (e.g., viruses, bacteria) or haematogenous seeding (e.g., HIV, TB). No vector‑borne life cycle is involved.
b: Mumps virus → parotid inflammation after respiratory spread
Staphylococcus aureus → acute suppurative sialadenitis after oral flora ascent

sections.p: Clinically important conditions include infectious sialadenitis, obstructive sialolithiasis, autoimmune Sjögren syndrome, and neoplastic lesions. In East African hospitals, HIV‑related salivary gland disease and tuberculous involvement are notable.
b: Acute bacterial sialadenitis – painful swelling, fever, purulent discharge
Chronic sialadenitis – recurrent swelling, often after meals
Sjögren syndrome – dry mouth, xerostomia, anti‑SSA/SSB antibodies
Mumps – bilateral parotid enlargement, especially in unvaccinated children
Tuberculous parotitis – firm mass, systemic TB signs, often misdiagnosed as tumour

sections.p: History, focused examination and targeted investigations differentiate infection, obstruction and autoimmune disease.

t.a: Clinical exam (inspection, palpation, sialography if available)
t.b: Identifies swelling pattern, tenderness, ductal discharge; distinguishes obstructive stones from inflammatory mass
Detects stones, abscesses, cystic changes; portable and affordable in low‑resource settings
Confirms Sjögren syndrome when clinical xerostomia present; not required for acute infection
Helps rule out malignancy when a firm mass persists; if unavailable, refer for surgical biopsy
Detects HIV‑associated salivary gland disease; essential in patients with unexplained bilateral enlargement

sections.p: Management follows a stepwise approach: treat the underlying cause, relieve obstruction, and support gland function.
b: Acute bacterial sialadenitis – IV/IV‑to‑oral ampicillin‑sulbactam or clindamycin (covers Staph and anaerobes); hydrate, massage gland, warm compresses
Obstructive sialolithiasis – encourage hydration, sour candy to stimulate flow; if stone >5 mm, refer for sialendoscopy or surgical removal
Sjögren syndrome – topical saliva substitutes, pilocarpine (muscarinic agonist) if available; monitor for dental caries
Mumps – supportive care, analgesia, isolation to prevent spread; vaccinate eligible contacts
TB parotitis – standard anti‑TB regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 6 months

t.b: Improves saliva flow, reduces stasis; essential when imaging unavailable
Reduces drooling in neurologic patients; consider only where toxin is stocked

sections.p: Key points examiners love: differentiate infectious vs obstructive swelling, recognise Sjögren’s oral findings, and know the limited investigations feasible in a district hospital.
b: Water‑brash (reflex salivation) signals gastro‑oesophageal reflux, not gland disease
Parotid pain worsens on chewing → sialolithiasis; pain at rest → infection
Bilateral painless enlargement in a young adult with HIV → consider HIV‑associated salivary gland disease

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly expanding neck swelling with airway compromise
High fever, neck rigidity, or signs of sepsis
Sudden loss of saliva with severe dehydration

faq.q: Why does xerostomia increase dental caries?
faq.a: Saliva buffers acid, provides calcium and antimicrobial IgA; loss of these defenses allows plaque bacteria to demineralise teeth.

faq.q: Can a stone be seen on plain X‑ray?
faq.a: Only if it contains calcium; most submandibular stones are radiolucent, so ultrasound is preferred.
No; treatment is symptomatic and aims to prevent complications such as dental decay and oral infections.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV presents with bilateral painless parotid swelling – what investigations would you order and why? — Order ultrasound to look for cystic change, HIV viral load, and anti‑SSA/SSB to exclude Sjögren; results guide whether to treat infection, refer for biopsy, or manage as HIV‑related disease.

A child with fever, unilateral parotid pain that worsens on chewing – what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Acute bacterial sialadenitis; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, hydrate, apply warm compresses, and massage the gland.

You suspect sialolithiasis but ultrasound is unavailable – how do you proceed? — Encourage high‑fluid intake, sour candy, gland massage; if pain persists, arrange referral for sialendoscopy or surgical removal.

A patient with dry mouth, positive anti‑SSA antibodies, and normal salivary gland ultrasound – what is the diagnosis and long‑term care? — Primary Sjögren syndrome; provide saliva substitutes, pilocarpine if available, and schedule regular dental reviews.

How does secretory IgA protect the oral cavity and why is its deficiency clinically important? — IgA neutralises microbes and prevents adherence to mucosa; deficiency predisposes to recurrent oral candidiasis and severe caries.

What features distinguish tuberculous parotitis from a malignant parotid tumour on examination? — TB often has systemic symptoms (weight loss, night sweats), a softer, fluctuant mass, and may respond to anti‑TB therapy; malignancy is usually firm, fixed, and progressive.

Why is ampicillin‑sulbactam preferred for acute bacterial sialadenitis in a low‑resource setting? — It covers the common pathogens (Staph aureus, anaerobes) in a single IV/PO regimen, reducing need for multiple drugs.

When is botulinum toxin indicated for salivary gland disease and what are its risks? — Used for refractory drooling in neurologic patients; risks include dry mouth, dysphagia, and transient weakness of nearby muscles.
